1:
The turn from Israel to the nations is noticed first. Gill says that having done prophesying to the Jews the prophet is bid to prophesy against the Gentiles, the nations lying nearest them. Keil and Delitzsch give the reason: while the prophet’s mouth was to be mute to Israel, the Lord directed him to foretell destruction to the heathen nations, so that they might not be lifted up by the fall of the people and kingdom of God but might recognise in the judgment upon Israel a work of the Judge of the whole earth. They also count what follows. Seven heathen nations have their destruction foretold here, Ammon, Moab, Edom and the Philistines, then Tyre and Sidon, and last Egypt; and the prophecies are divided by the introductory formula into thirteen words of God, the first four nations comprehended in one, four separate words directed against Tyre, one against Sidon and seven against Egypt. In the seven nations and the seven words against Egypt they cannot fail to discover an allusion to the symbolical significance of the number. Clarke gives the same list and adds that these threatenings were fulfilled by Nebuchadnezzar about five years after the destruction of Jerusalem, the chronological place of the chapter being later than its position.

Setting the face is taken by Gill and Henry as a matter of bearing. Gill has the prophet look towards where the Ammonites lived and put on a frowning, menacing countenance, noting that some versions render the command as strengthen thy face, that is, look boldly at them. Henry makes the gesture representative: in setting his face against them the prophet signifies that God sets his face against them, for the face of the Lord is against those that do evil. He must therefore speak with boldness, as one who knew whose errand he went upon, setting his face as a flint and facing down enemies who were very impudent.

Who these enemies were Ellicott sets out most fully, taking the utterances against the four neighbouring nations as one prophecy spoken after Jerusalem fell. The Ammonites, descended from Lot, had been persistent enemies of Israel for centuries: they joined the Moabites under Eglon and were subdued by Jephthah, fought with cruelty and insolence against Saul, were crushed by David, had their idolatries favoured by Solomon, failed in an attack under Jehoshaphat, paid tribute to Uzziah and Jotham, and had lately occupied the vacant cities of Gad; now they had joined the army of Nebuchadnezzar. Their hostility, Ellicott concludes, arose not only from national jealousy but from an especial hatred of the Jewish religion. Gill says the same briefly: implacable enemies who hated the religion of the Jews and envied their wealth. Clarke supplies the occasion: Nebuchadnezzar, in doubt whether to besiege the Ammonite capital or Jerusalem first, was determined by divination to attack Jerusalem, whereupon the Ammonites, seeing the success of his arms, made friends with him and exulted in the ruin of the Jews.

How the word reached them is answered two ways. Gill supposes it delivered to their ambassadors or merchants at Babylon, or by letters, the prophet being in Chaldea at a distance from them. Henry takes the opposite view of the same distance: the prophet had been a captive in Babylon for many years and knew little of his own nation, much less of the nations about it, but God told him both what they were doing and what he was about to do with them, so that he speaks as pertinently as if he had been among them. Wesley states the charge in a line: when they should have pitied they proudly insulted over the people of God. Clarke notes that although the fulfilment is not recorded in Scripture, Josephus reports that Nebuchadnezzar afterwards turned his arms against the Ammonites and Moabites and then against Egypt, Berosus adding Syria and Arabia.
4:
Who the men of the east are is answered four ways. Gill canvasses three: the Chaldeans and Syrians on the east side, as Jarchi has it, the Medes and Persians further east, as Kimchi, or, as he thinks likelier, the Arabians, who formed part of the army of Nebuchadnezzar and might be rewarded with this country. Wesley settles on the last without hesitation, the Arabians being associates of Nebuchadnezzar who recompensed their service with the land once conquered, five years after the desolation of Jerusalem. Clarke names particular tribes, the Scenite Arabs and Ishmaelites and people of Kedar, who seized the provinces of the vanquished Ammonites, and argues that the description can suit no other people, since these lived on fruits and the milk of their flocks and used camels; some, he notes, take the phrase for the Chaldeans instead. Ellicott keeps the phrase general, rendering it literally as sons of the east and taking it of the nomadic tribes of the eastern deserts who occupy the country to this day; and he adds a distinction the others do not draw, that they are possessors of the land and not conquerors, the conquest itself being effected by Nebuchadnezzar.

Ellicott also corrects a rendering and fills in the sequel. The word given as palaces properly means an enclosure for folding cattle, and where it is used elsewhere of desert tribes it is translated castles, which he calls a singularly inappropriate sense; it came afterwards to mean a dwelling-place of any kind. He takes the Ammonites and Moabites to have practically constituted one nation, the Moabites the settled and the Ammonites the nomadic portion, and observes that after the conquest the Ammonites gradually dwindled away until lost from history. Clarke says the same in a sentence: except in history the name of the Ammonites does not now exist.

The camels in the royal city are taken literally by all three. Gill has the Arabians pitch their tents about Rabbath, the metropolis of Ammon, and convert its houses and even its palaces into stables; Ellicott says the city, the only important town the Ammonites had, has become literally a stable for the camels of wandering Bedouins, and notes that in the parallel clause the people are put for the land they inhabit, as Wesley also observes. On the later site the three differ: Gill reports from Jerom that in his day it was called Philadelphia, after Ptolemy Philadelphus, who rebuilt it; Wesley says it was named from the king of Egypt who built it; Ellicott says the Ptolemies founded the city on the site of Rabbah, that extensive ruins there belong to the Roman occupation, and that the Ammonites had no part in either of those cities, the place being now utterly without inhabitants, so that the most recent traveller could describe its striking characteristic as lonely desolation in a rich country.

The closing formula divides the readers sharply. Ellicott observes that this frequent close of the denunciations against Israel is used here at the end of each message in the chapter, and insists that it refers not to any penitent recognition of the Lord but to an experience of his wrath so plain that they can no longer refuse to acknowledge his power. Wesley takes it the other way, that God will thus bring those who were strangers to him into acquaintance with him, a blessed effect of their calamities, since it is much better to be poor and know God than to be rich and ignorant of him. Gill reads the stretched-out hand as just retaliation for the hands they had clapped against his people, and one they could neither resist nor bear. Ellicott adds a note on the word rendered spoil, which occurs only here and which the margin gives as meat or food, the figure seeming the same as that which speaks of devouring a people.
8:
The sin charged against Moab is the one charged against Ammon, stated at different depths. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a misunderstanding and despising of the divine election of Israel: when Judah was overthrown, the malicious assertion that the house of Judah was like all the heathen nations meant that it had no pre-eminence over them and shared the same fate. Wesley says the same in a phrase, that they are no more a select people than others. Henry divides the triumph in two. They triumphed first in the apostasies of Israel, pleased to see them forsake their God and worship idols and hoping their religion would in a while be quite lost; and Henry draws the lesson that when those who profess religion walk unworthy of their profession they encourage its enemies to hope it will sink and be abandoned. They triumphed secondly in the calamities of Israel, saying that their God was no more able to deliver them from this overflowing scourge than the gods of the heathen, and asking where were the promises they gloried in and the wonders their fathers had told of.

Why Seir stands beside Moab is remarked on by several, Keil and Delitzsch calling it remarkable. Henry notes that Seir, the seat of the Edomites, is joined with Moab because they said the same thing, though reckoned with separately a few verses later; Ellicott makes the same observation. Clarke adds a political ground for the group: Moab and Edom, with the Ammonites, had made a league with Zedekiah which they did not keep, and are supposed even to have joined the Chaldeans. Ellicott sets Moab beside Ammon: sprung from the same source, closely associated with it in history and denounced in nearly the same prophecies, it was the more settled and stronger people, lay immediately to the south, and also contributed its quota to the armies of Nebuchadnezzar.

The opening of Moab’s side is glossed the same way by all. Gill renders it the shoulder, where their greatest strength lay; Clarke calls it the strongest frontier place and names Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon and Kiriathaim as frontier towns; Wesley calls it simply the part best fortified. Ellicott alone gives the cities a history. They lay north of the Arnon and had been wrested from the Moabites by the Amorites before the time of Moses, taken in turn by the Israelites, and long formed part of Israel’s territory, until in the decay of Israel’s power Moab re-conquered them; they are named here, he suggests, as rightfully a possession of Israel and so the fitting point from which desolation should go out over the whole country. As for the glory of the land, the territory these three cities mark is still reckoned by the Arabs the best part of it and called Belka, of which they have a proverb that no land can be found like it.

Ellicott complains that the division between the verses seriously obscures the sense, which is that God will throw open Moab as well as Ammon to the sons of the east and give both into their possession, so that Ammon shall be remembered no more and judgment be executed on Moab; and he keeps his earlier distinction, that the two were conquered by Nebuchadnezzar but possessed by the Bedouins. Gill reads it as a way made for the same people of the east who had destroyed Ammon to enter Moab and possess it likewise; Wesley says the Chaldeans will give it to the Arabians. Clarke notes a variant reading the clause as a threat that Rabbah of the sons of Ammon be not remembered. Gill closes on the agency: though the Chaldeans and Arabians were the instruments, the destruction was of the Lord; and though God had spoken against his own people in his providence and chastised them for their sins, he will not suffer others to speak against them.
12:
Edom is charged with something worse than the two nations before it, and Keil and Delitzsch mark the difference. The Ammonites and Moabites are charged with nothing more than malicious pleasure at the fall of Israel and disregard of its divine calling, whereas the Edomites are reproached with revengeful acts of hostility towards the house of Judah and threatened with extermination in consequence; the doing of Edom is more precisely defined as consisting in the taking of vengeance, and is designated as very guilty. Clarke says the same without the analysis: the Edomites were the most inveterate enemies of the Jews from the earliest times and ever did all they could to annoy them. Gill notes only that the usage was base and barbarous from a people who were originally brethren.

Ellicott traces the grudge to its root and follows it down. The reason of the hostility is expressly said to be revenge; descended from the elder son, the Edomites had never looked complacently on the spiritual superiority given to the descendants of the younger. They showed it from the first in refusing, with a show of violence, a passage to the Israelites through their territory, and though subdued and made tributary under David and Solomon, in the decline of Jewish power they took every opportunity for hostility. At this time, Ellicott says, they not only joined the armies of Nebuchadnezzar but appear to have urged the conqueror on to greater cruelty and to have waylaid the fugitives themselves to cut them off; and during the captivity they took possession of many towns of Judea, Hebron among them, which were recovered only in the time of the Maccabees.

The two place-names of the threat are identified three ways, and one of them oddly. Ellicott takes Teman, a word meaning south, for a southern district of Edom famed for its wisdom, and says Dedan is frequently mentioned by the prophets but in such a way that it has not been certainly identified; he proposes a better rendering of the clause, from Teman unto Dedan, meaning from one end of the country to the other they shall fall by the sword. Wesley agrees in substance, calling Teman a country on the southern coast of Edom and Dedan a place adjoining it. Clarke calls them both cities of the Moabites, apparently at either extremity of the land, which puts them in the wrong nation for a threat against Edom, though his sense of the phrase, that it spans the country from end to end, is the same as the others.

How the vengeance was executed is agreed and its meaning disputed. Gill refers the fulfilment to the times of the Maccabees, when the Edomites were overthrown and conquered. Clarke says the same and adds the detail that the conquerors not only defeated them and brought them under complete subjection but obliged them to receive circumcision. Ellicott names the conqueror as John Hyrcanus and gives the sequel: they were compelled to submit to circumcision as a mark of absorption into the Jewish people, and afterwards Herod, himself of Idumean origin, reigned over them as king of the Jews, and their name disappeared from history. On what that absorption signifies Ellicott parts company with others. Many commentators, he says, would see in the prophecy a further intimation of the ultimate conversion of Edom and its incorporation into the Church; but this seems to him quite foreign, not only to the scope of this whole series of prophecies, but especially to the connection in which it stands, since the passage says that God will lay his vengeance upon Edom and that they shall know his vengeance. Clarke draws a different moral from the same words, that God will not allow men to insult those whom he has cast down, since his judgment is sufficient and to add anything to it is an insult to God himself.
15:
The last of the four is charged with both of the sins already named. Keil and Delitzsch say the Philistines resembled the Edomites in their thirst for revenge and the Ammonites in their malicious rejoicing at the fall of Israel, so that the description of their sin here is a combination of elements taken from the conduct of both, executing revenge with contempt in the soul. For that reason, they add, Isaiah had already classed the Philistines with Edom and Moab and Ammon as enemies who would be successfully attacked and overcome by Israel when the Lord had gathered it again from its dispersion. Gill introduces them simply as another enemy of the people of Israel who had been of old an implacable one, and reads the sentence as retaliation for their vengeance and fury and malice against God’s people, the judgments upon them being very great in both quantity and quality.

Why they came under the sword at this particular time is answered differently. Clarke gives an immediate occasion, that Nebuchadnezzar punished them because they had assisted the Tyrians while he was besieging their city, and observes that the several lordships of the Philistines occupied the coast of the Mediterranean from Judea to Egypt. Ellicott makes it a matter of long attrition rather than of one offence. The historical books are almost a continuous record of Philistine hostility, and at times they held the greater part of the land of Israel in subjection and at times were subdued in their turn; although they belonged to another branch of the Hamitic family, their land was included with that of the Canaanites in the territory to be given to the Israelites, and yet it was never occupied by them, though some of the kings fortified and garrisoned the cities. Lying as it did along the coast on the highway between Egypt and Assyria, that land meant that in the struggles of the great powers with one another the Philistines were gradually more and more reduced, until they disappeared entirely.

The Cherethim are identified two ways. Ellicott takes them for a portion of the Philistines living on their southern coast, whose name is sometimes put for the whole nation; many suppose it equivalent to Cretans and take it as indicating that the Philistines came originally from the island of Crete, though Ellicott calls the etymology doubtful. He offers another reason for the name appearing just here, that there was probably a play upon words in the original, the phrase rendered I will cut off the Cherethim reading rather I will slay the slayers. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause with the Cretan identification taken for granted, cutting off the Cretans and destroying the remnant by the seashore. Wesley takes the word quite otherwise, making the Cherethim the bowmen, the strength of Philistia.

What remnant is left to destroy is also read two ways. Wesley makes it historical and specific, those who had escaped the sword of Samuel, of David, of Hezekiah, and of Psammetichus king of Egypt; Ellicott has already accounted for the wearing away without naming any of those, by the position of the land between contending empires. Gill for his part rests the whole on the malice and despiteful usage that provoked it, and Keil and Delitzsch close where the chapter closes, with the vengeance executed through chastisements of wrath so that they shall know that the Lord has brought it upon them.
